content: Pokeweed, also referred to as poke, poke bush, pokeberry, pokeroot, polk salad, polk sallet, inkberry, or ombú, belongs to the genus Phytolacca. These are perennial plants native to regions such as North America, South America, East Asia, and New Zealand. The plant contains toxic compounds, including phytolaccatoxin and phytolaccigenin, which are harmful to mammals. However, birds consume the berries without adverse effects because the seeds, protected by their hard outer shells, pass through the digestive system intact and are excreted whole. Pokeweed plants typically grow to heights ranging from 1 to 10 feet. They feature single, alternate leaves with pointed tips and crinkled edges. The stems are often pink or red in color. The flowers are greenish-white and grow in elongated clusters at the ends of the stems, eventually developing into dark purple berries. One species, Phytolacca dioica (commonly known as ombú), grows as a tree in the pampas of South America and serves as one of the few sources of shade in the open grasslands. This tree is a cultural symbol of Argentina and gaucho traditions. Young pokeweed leaves can be boiled three times, with the water discarded after each boiling, to reduce the toxin levels. The resulting dish, known as poke sallet or poke salad, is occasionally available commercially. However, many experts caution against consuming pokeweed even after this preparation, as trace amounts of toxins may still remain. Despite medical warnings, poke salad has cultural significance, particularly in Southern U.S. cuisine, and was popularized in the 1969 song Polk Salad Annie by Tony Joe White, later famously covered by Elvis Presley. Pokeberry juice is sometimes added to other juices for making jelly, as some believe it alleviates arthritis pain. Pokeweed has also been used in homeopathic remedies for various ailments. It can be applied topically for conditions like acne or taken internally for issues such as tonsillitis, swollen glands, and weight loss. Native Americans historically used grated pokeroot as a poultice to treat breast inflammations and rashes. The berries of pokeweed yield a red ink or dye, which Native Americans once used to decorate their horses. Notably, the Declaration of Independence of the United States was written using fermented pokeberry juice, giving rise to the common name inkberry. During the Civil War, letters written with pokeberry ink have survived, with the writing appearing brown over time. The red juice has also been used symbolically, such as in anti-slavery protests by Benjamin Lay. A rich brown dye can be created by fermenting the berries and soaking fabrics in the resulting liquid. Some varieties of pokeweed are cultivated as ornamental plants, primarily for their attractive berries. Certain cultivars have been selected for their larger fruit clusters. Additionally, pokeweed serves as a food source for the larvae of some Lepidoptera species, including the Giant Leopard Moth. The toxic components of pokeweed include saponins, which are believed to be the primary toxic agents, as well as the alkaloids phytolaccine and phytolaccotoxin, and a glycoprotein. If consumed as food, the water used for boiling must be discarded to reduce toxicity. Clinical signs of pokeweed poisoning can vary depending on the quantity ingested. Nonfatal amounts may cause symptoms such as retching or vomiting after two or more hours, followed by difficulty breathing, sweating, spasms, severe diarrhea (often bloody), prostration, tremors, and sometimes convulsions. In cases of fatal poisoning, which may occur if roots are consumed, these symptoms progress to respiratory paralysis and other narcotic effects, ultimately leading to death. Additional signs include colic, respiratory failure, unsteadiness, inability to rise, jerking movements of the legs, subnormal body temperature, and a decrease in milk production in lactating animals.
